content: Miliaria, also known as prickly heat or sweat rash, is a dermatological condition characterized by the appearance of small, itchy rashes. It is particularly prevalent in hot and humid climates, such as tropical regions or during the summer months. While it can affect individuals of all ages, it is especially common in children and infants due to the immaturity of their sweat glands. The pathophysiology of miliaria involves the obstruction of sweat gland ducts, which can occur due to the accumulation of dead skin cells or the presence of bacteria, such as Staphylococcus epidermidis. This bacterium, commonly found on the skin, is also associated with acne. The blockage of sweat ducts leads to the trapping of sweat beneath the skin, resulting in irritation, itching, and the formation of small blisters in localized areas. Certain medications, such as diflorasone, may increase the risk of developing miliaria. Clinically, miliaria presents with small red papules that may itch or cause an intense pins-and-needles sensation. These rashes can appear on various parts of the body, including the face, neck, under the breasts, and the scrotum. Other commonly affected areas include skin folds and regions prone to friction with clothing, such as the back, chest, and abdomen. A related condition, folliculitis, may occur simultaneously, involving inflammation of hair follicles due to blockage by foreign material. It is important to differentiate miliaria from shingles, as both conditions can present with similar symptoms. Shingles, however, typically affects only one side of the body and is accompanied by pain and a prickling sensation. Prompt medical attention is advised for suspected shingles, as early antiviral treatment is crucial. Miliaria is classified based on the depth of sweat gland obstruction. The mildest form, miliaria crystallina, involves superficial obstruction and manifests as tiny, asymptomatic, blister-like lesions resembling beads of sweat. The most common form, miliaria rubra, results from deeper obstruction, leading to sweat leakage into the epidermis and triggering an inflammatory response. This form is characterized by redness, larger blister-like lesions, intense itching, and reduced sweating (anhidrosis) in the affected areas. Severe cases of miliaria rubra may pose a risk of heat exhaustion, particularly if a large surface area of the body is involved or if the individual continues heat-producing activities. The most severe form, miliaria profunda, arises as a complication of recurrent episodes of miliaria rubra. In this form, the obstruction occurs deep within the sweat gland structure, causing sweat to leak between the superficial and deeper layers of the skin. The rash in miliaria profunda is typically flesh-colored rather than red and may appear within hours of activities that provoke sweating, resolving similarly when the stimulus is removed. This form carries a higher risk of heat exhaustion. Prevention of miliaria involves minimizing activities that induce sweating, using air conditioning to cool the environment, wearing lightweight clothing, and avoiding hot and humid conditions. If these measures are not feasible, frequent showers to cleanse and unblock sweat glands are recommended. Treatment for miliaria generally involves supportive care, as the condition often resolves without intervention. However, severe cases may persist for weeks and cause significant discomfort. General recommendations include moving to a cooler environment, avoiding activities that provoke sweating, and wearing non-occlusive clothing. Frequent cool showers are also beneficial. Topical antibacterial agents, such as antibacterial soaps, may help reduce the duration of symptoms in miliaria rubra, even in the absence of overt superinfection. Anti-itch preparations, such as calamine or menthol and camphor-based products, and topical steroid creams may alleviate symptoms, but caution is advised with oil-based formulations, as they may exacerbate sweat gland blockage. Other treatments, including supplemental vitamins A and C or vitamin A-based medications, have been investigated, but there is limited scientific evidence supporting their efficacy in reducing symptom duration or preventing complications. If the rash progresses to open blisters or pustular lesions, medical consultation is necessary to rule out other conditions and determine if more aggressive treatment is required.
